פ\"ק דמציע' דף י' וכ\"כ המרדכי אבל דעת הנימוקי יוסף דאפי' לא ידע השליח נמי אין שלד\"ע ופטור המשלח. ובש\"ך האריך בזה להוכיח כדברי הנ\"י וז\"ל ועוד דע\"כ מה שהוציאו כן מהמשנה דפ' מרובה כפי פירש\"י אין פי' המשנה כן דא\"כ למה ליה לתלמוד' להקשות פ\"ק דמציע' דף י\"א אריש לקיש דאמר חצר משום שליחות אתרבאי ומשמע דלר' יוחנן לא קשה מידי והא בלא\"ה תיקשי כן אמתני' דמרובה אפי' בלא בריית' דהמצ' תמצא כו' וכמו רש\"י שכת' בכל התורה כולה דאשלד\"ע והעושה מתחייב ואע\"ג דלא ידע שליח דהא גבי מעילה השליח לא ידע ואי נימ' דהיכ' דלא ידע יש שליחות לד\"ע א\"כ בנזכר בעה\"ב אמאי מעל השליח כיון דלא ידע השליח וה\"ל כעושה תוס' והמרדכי צ\"ל כטעמ' דרש\"י בחגיגה ואע\"ג דדברים שבלב לאו דברים כיון דאנן סהדי בביטולו ה\"ל דברים שבלב כל אדם דהוי דברים ועמ\"ש בסי' י\"ב סק\"א. ובחילוף הטעמים שכת' רש\"י בקידושין ובחגיגה בצ\"ע ועכ\"פ למדנו מדברי רש\"י בקידושין דאשלד\"ע אפילו היכא דלא ידע. ולכן נראה לענ\"ד לולי דברי תוס' במה דקשי' להו דהיכי מתחייב הגנב במשיכת השומר הא אשלד\"ע נראה דרש\"י לטעמיה דס\"ל פ\"ק דמציעא (דף ח') גבי שותפין שגנבו דהיכ' דעושה שליח לגנוב אדעתיה ואדחבריה יש שליח לדבר עבירה מגו דזכי לנפשיה זכי נמי לחברי' ועמ\"ש בסק\"ד וכיון דשומרין בעי משיכה ובלא משיכה לא מחייבי וכמ\"ש הרמב\"ם וש\"ע בסי' רצ\"א ומש\"ה כשנתנו הגנב לשומר מגו דזכי לנפשיה להתחייב בדין שמירה זכי נמי לחבריה והיינו שיקנה הגנב להתחייב באונסין דכיון דזכי לנפשיה במשיכה זו זכי נמי לחבריה וזה נכון ודו\"ק. וניח' בזה ליישב פרש\"י שם דקשי' טוב' שם בגמ' (דף ע\"ט) דבעי אמימר אי תקנו משיכה בשומרים ואמרינן עלה ת\"ש נתנו לבכורות בנו לש\"ח כו' ש\"מ תיקנו משיכה בשומרים כו' וכיון דלפרש\"י מיירי בגנב שיתחייב הגנב וא\"כ ודאי בעי משיכה דאם לא משך נהי שהשומר יתחייב בלא משיכה הגנב אינו מתחייב אלא במשיכת השומר שהוא שלוחו וע\"ש בתורת חיים. ולפמ\"ש ניחא דאם שומרים לא בעי משיכה גם הגנב לא מתחייב במשיכת השומר כיון דאשלד\"ע ומגו דזכי לנפשיה לא שייך ביה כיון דאמרת שומרים לא בעי משיכה אע\"כ תיקנו משיכה בשומרים ואמרינן ביה מגו דזכי לנפשיה ונתנו לבכורות בנו או לבע\"ח לא מיירי שנתנו לגמרי אלא שנתנו אפותיקי וכמ\"ש תוס' שם ד\"ה תיקנו משיכה בשומרים ע\"ש וא\"כ ה\"ל נמי שומר ואמרינן ביה מגו דזכי לנפשיה וכמ\"ש וא\"כ שפיר מצי איירי שידע השומר והתוס' שהקשו הא אין שלד\"ע לטעמיה פ\"ק דמציע' דף ח' דמשמע מדבריהם דלא אמרינן בשלד\"ע מגו דזכה לנפשיה. וראיה ברורה נראה דאפי' היכא דלא ידע שליח נמי אין שלד\"ע מהא דאמרינן בהמניח (דף ל\"ב) מתיב רבא הוסיף לו רצועה אחת ומת ה\"ז גולה על ידו והא הכא דשוגג קרוב למזיד הוא דאיבעי אסוקי אדעתיה דמייתי אינשי בחדא רצועה וקתני ה\"ז גולה אמר רב שימי מנהרדעא דטעי במניינא טפח ליה רבא בסנדל' א\"ל אטו הוא מני והתניא גדול שבדיינים קורא והשני מונה והג' אומר הכהו דלא אמר רב שימי מנהרדעא דטע' דיינא גופיה וע\"ש ואי נימא דהיכ' דהשליח לא ידע שלוחו כמותו אפילו לדבר עבירה א\"כ שליח ב\"ד אמאי גולה כיון דאינו אלא שליח ב\"ד והב\"ד הוא המשלחו ואע\"ג דהמשלח נמי לא ידע וכדמוכח מתוספת פרק האיש מקדש שהקשו למה לי קרא גבי מעילה דמשלח מעל תיפוק ליה דשליח לא ידע ע\"ש ואע\"ג דהתם המשלח לא ידע. ואם כן התם בשליח בית דין כיון דאינו אלא שליח ב\"ד אלא ודאי דאפי' בשוגג נמי אין שליח לדבר עבירה ומשום הכי שליח בית דין גולה ואף ע\"ג דבגניבה אם השליח שוגג ודאי פטור השליח היינו משום דבגניבה אינו מחייב בשוגג אבל גלות חייב על השוגג והשליח הוא דחייב וזה ראיה ברורה ודו\"ק:"]
ketzot_hachoshen.en:
There is no agency for a transgression. Rashi holds that where one participant lifts stolen property both for himself and for his partner, the partner can acquire through the principle that since the lifter acquires for himself, he can also acquire for his partner. This applies even in the setting of wrongdoing. Tosafot appears to require that both partners physically lift. I find that difficult. Even when both lift, the reason the act works for each is still that each effective acquisition can extend to the other. If that principle can operate despite the transgression, there is no reason it should fail where one alone lifts for both. Rashi's treatment of slaughter by one partner for both differs because slaughter is not an acquisition act. The special liability for slaughter or sale requires the Torah's independent extension to an agent. The principle that "since he acquires for himself, he acquires for his fellow" applies to acquisitive acts such as lifting, purchase, theft, or robbery, not to a later slaughter that merely generates statutory liability. Therefore, where one partner performs the acquisition act of theft for both, Rashi's rule can make both liable through the shared acquisition. For the later slaughter, the separate special verse is needed.
The agent is not himself subject to liability. The Gemara discusses a thief who tells a custodian to remove an ox from the owner's domain. Rashi explains that the thief becomes liable through the custodian's meshichah even though ordinarily there is no agency for transgression. Tosafot answers that the custodian does not know the ox is stolen, so he resembles a courtyard that acquires involuntarily. Nimukei Yosef disagrees and holds that even an unaware agent does not create ordinary agency for transgression. The Shach supports Nimukei Yosef and argues that if Rashi meant actual agency, the same problem would have arisen in the Gemara's own analysis of the Mishnah. But the sugya can be explained differently. At an earlier stage, the Mishnah can be established where the thief himself stole from a custodian. Only later, under Rav Ashi's reading, does Rashi's explanation become necessary. Still, Rashi himself elsewhere clearly holds that there is no agency for transgression even when the agent did not know. In Kiddushin, if the principal remembers that the money is consecrated but the agent remains unaware, the agent commits misuse. Rashi explains that throughout the Torah there is no agency for transgression and the actor bears liability, even though the agent was ignorant. This directly supports Nimukei Yosef. How, then, can Rashi here make the thief liable through the custodian's meshichah? The answer follows Rashi's rule regarding partners who steal. Custodianship itself requires meshichah. When the unaware custodian pulls the ox, he acquires for himself the custodial status. Since that same act is a valid acquisition for himself, it can also acquire for the thief under the principle that one who acquires for himself can acquire for another. This is not ordinary agency for transgression. This also explains the Gemara's inference that custodianship requires meshichah. If custodians did not need meshichah, the custodian's act would not be an acquisition for himself, and the principle extending it to the thief would disappear. A further proof that ignorance does not create agency for transgression comes from the case of the beit din agent who mistakenly administers one extra lash and thereby causes death. The court's agent is himself exiled for the unintended killing. If ignorance made him merely an extension of the court, his own liability would not arise. Thus even an unaware agent ordinarily remains the actor for transgression.

Shimon must return it to him, for why should he enter, etc. Meaning, even if Shimon has some claim against the relative explaining why she took the property, since he himself does not know whether her claim is true, he had no right to enter another person's house and assist her in removing it. This applies even though there were no witnesses to the removal. This is implied by Shimon's answer cited by the Tur and Mechaber, "It is true that I removed, etc." The phrase "it is true" implies that without his own admission Reuven could not have established the fact through witnesses. The preceding law is different. There Shimon did not enter and assist in the theft; rather, Reuven sued him because the stolen item later came into his possession and he returned it to the thief. Although the Tur there implies that the factual incident also involved Shimon entering and assisting with removal, it gives other reasons to exempt him for that act: the thief had already lifted the item and could have removed it alone, and Shimon further claimed that he knew the thief's position was correct. See there and examine carefully.
Some say that the sender is liable, because here one cannot say that the sender assumed the agent would refuse to do what he requested on the principle, "the words of the master and the words of the student, whose words should one obey?" since the agent himself is not legally liable. Darkei Moshe cites Mordechai in the first chapter of Bava Metzia in Maharam's name: if one tells another, "Acquire for me the ox in so-and-so's house, for it is mine," and it later turns out not to have been his and that he intended theft, the sender becomes responsible for the ox upon the agent's meshichah, because the agent did not know it was stolen property. Nimukei Yosef, in chapter Merubah, however, writes that the agent is liable, because there is no agency for a transgression even where the agent did not know that the act was prohibited.

Some say the sender is liable. See Shach, seif katan 6, who challenges Darkei Moshe for citing Nimukei Yosef as though the messenger himself is liable, since Nimukei Yosef does not say so and, if the messenger acted unknowingly, there is no obvious basis for personal liability. In my view Darkei Moshe means that the messenger can become liable to the owner under the ordinary laws of custodians. If, for example, he received the animal with borrower liability and it died, he can be liable to the true owner, just as where a renter lends the rented cow onward and the second borrower can become liable to the owner. Nimukei Yosef indeed writes in that direction. Still, the matter requires study. In an ordinary rental the renter has acquired a valid use-right and can transfer that use-right to a borrower, so the second person's meshichah creates borrower liability. Here the thief never acquired the object. How can he create a valid borrower relationship in favor of another person, especially according to the view that custodial liability requires meshichah and that an unauthorized borrower does not become liable merely from taking until actual use? Shach also seeks to reject Tosafot's principle that where the agent acts inadvertently there can be agency for a transgression. Ketzot HaChoshen likewise adduces the case of a beit din agent who added one lash beyond the authorized count and was liable to exile despite acting inadvertently. In my view that is not a proof. Even where agency for a transgression exists, Torah's novelty is ordinarily to impose liability on the sender, not to exempt the agent from liability that would have existed had he acted on his own. Where the agent's own act independently creates liability, he can remain liable even though the sender is also charged. Shelichut yad differs because the act requires an acquisition. Once Torah makes the acquisition operate for the sender, there may be no separate acquisition left for the agent. Me'ilah is similar: once the sender commits me'ilah through the agent's act and the item thereby leaves hekdesh, the agent may no longer be consuming hekdesh property. Likewise, in slaughter or sale after theft, the special fourfold or fivefold liability belongs to the original thief rather than to a later agent. This explains why the beit din messenger can incur exile. If he had delivered the extra blow on his own, he would have been liable, and the rule of agency does not erase that independent liability. It would have been stronger to ask why the judges themselves are not liable to exile as senders. That too is not decisive, because judges are not liable to exile merely for an erroneous judicial ruling. For capital liability, however, it is clear that a sender is not executed merely because an unwitting agent performed a capital transgression. We do not find a rule that one who tells another to violate Shabbat unknowingly becomes liable to death through the other's act. The derivation that sometimes imposes liability on a sender through an agent who is not personally subject to the prohibition comes from theft-related cases and does not automatically extend from lashes to death. Tosafot in Shevuot imply that where the agent himself is not subject to the prohibition, even a non Jew can sometimes create liability for the sender. This does not mean that telling a non Jew to cook on Shabbat becomes a d'oraisa violation. That principle applies when the prohibited result occurs in the Jewish sender himself, such as a kohen arranging a prohibited marriage or causing a Jew's prohibited haircut. When the non Jew merely cooks on Shabbat, no prohibited act has occurred in the Jewish sender's body or property at that time. As for me'ilah and the case of Yoav, an unwitting agent is still considered a person subject to the law because inadvertence itself can require atonement. One who acts based on another's statement must still investigate where Torah expects him to do so. A woman who remarries based on one witness can be liable for a korban, and Yoav could not simply rely on David where Shaul's servants themselves refused a comparable order. By contrast, where a thief tells another person to take an item from the owner's domain, the recipient can accept it into custody in order to save it from theft. At the moment of taking he need not yet investigate in the same manner, because if he refuses the thief will simply take it himself. Receiving it to preserve it can itself be a mitzvah of returning lost property. Therefore Tosafot can say that the ordinary rule of "the Master's words precede the student's" does not defeat agency at the initial taking in that case.

שמשמע מדברי מהרש\"ל שם שהראב\"ד מפרש המשנה כרש\"י ליתא דנהי דהראב\"ד לא מפרש כהרמב\"ם מ\"מ גם כרש\"י לא מפרש ע\"ש מבואר כך בדבריו להדי' במ\"ש ואף לאו בגנב אלא מילתא באפי' נפשי' קאמר ע\"ש ונראה דלהכי siftei_kohen.en:
One who shows another person where to steal, or sends him, etc. The authorities discuss one who sends another to steal, but not one who merely points out the place of the theft. The Rama combined the two because Darkei Moshe cites Terumat HaDeshen regarding Reuven, who showed a notorious thief where Levi's tunnel was so that he could steal from it. Reuven is exempt because this is indirect causation. This ruling is necessary even according to the view that agency applies where the agent is not legally liable, for the person who merely points out the property remains exempt as a remote cause. It is also necessary according to the view that the sender is always exempt because there is no agency for transgression. One might have thought that, as in the law of one who reveals another's property to a gentile, he is liable under the law of direct causation even without agency. Terumat HaDeshen therefore teaches that this case is only indirect causation and not legally direct damage.
Some say that the sender, etc. I do not know why the Rama presents this as merely 'some say,' since Darkei Moshe cites no dissent. Nevertheless, as I explained in siman 182, the derivation from Hagahot Maimoniyot and the Mordechai is not compelling. In my view there is no distinction between an agent who is legally liable and one who is not. There is never agency for transgression, except in the special case of a courtyard. Darkei Moshe and the Sema cite the Mordechai regarding one who said, 'Take for me the ox in that house, for it is mine,' when in truth he intended the agent to steal it. The sender is said to become liable when the innocent agent draws the ox into his possession. The Nimukei Yosef rules that the sender remains exempt even where the agent did not know he was committing a prohibition. The agent himself is plainly exempt where he was unaware, as Yam Shel Shlomo states. Maharshal attacks the Nimukei Yosef and compares the innocent agent to a courtyard. This comparison is not correct. The phrase 'not legally liable' refers to a person who is intrinsically outside the prohibition, whereas here the agent is a person subject to the prohibition and merely lacks knowledge. Likewise, the principle that the agent could choose whether to act refers to his objective ability to act or refrain, which exists here. Had the Gemara intended to distinguish inadvertence from intent, it would have said so explicitly. The Mishna concerning slaughter by another person does not establish liability of a sender through an innocent human agent. Most commentators explain that Mishna differently, and the Raavad does not adopt Rashi's interpretation. The case of David and Joab also supports the Nimukei Yosef. Joab acted under a mistake, believing Uriah liable as one who rebelled against the king, yet the Gemara still treats the question under the rule that there is no agency for transgression. Shammai the Elder holds David liable only because he maintains agency for transgression generally, or because Scripture specifically states, 'You killed him with the sword of the children of Ammon.' According to the Sages, David was exempt from earthly liability; the Gemara's need to describe Uriah as a rebel concerns punishment in Heaven, not legal agency. The same principle is evident from misuse of consecrated property, which is fundamentally inadvertent, yet the Gemara still requires a special verse to impose liability on the sender. The better conclusion is therefore that even where the agent is unaware, the sender is exempt because there is no agency for transgression, while the innocent agent is also exempt.
